units.translation: you do not boast this word over one who lies low
for fear is now boasted at the gates
who struck him with the boasts of the high-speaking
the boasts of mighty men have fallen
what marriage do you boast of?
the boast thinks not as a man
not holding a boast in his hands
such a boast, full of truth, is not shameful
a din at the gates of bronze-bound shields
of the knee pressing on the dust
to cover with dust; to hasten
lest great wealth (a great deity, Heimsoeth) having stirred up the dust with its foot overturn prosperity
the Argive army advances, it raises dust
Thus I corrected the corrupt reading in M, δόσως κόνις [giving dust].
the ethereal dust appearing persuades me
when the earthy dust drinks the dark-clotted blood
and the thirsty dust, sister of the mud, bears witness to these things
but when the dust has drawn up the blood of a man
the dust having drunk the black blood of the citizens
I see dust, the voiceless messenger of the army
wretched ones, they clothed themselves with Ossaean dust

and corruptly κονώεῖν: συνιέναι, ἐπίστασθαι [to understand, to know]. No examples of the writers besides Aeschylus exist, but some of the cognate forms κοᾶν and κοεῖν, with the meaning of hearing or understanding, about which see Thes. vol. 4 p. 1097.
where M has εὐγακόννις, which is corrected from the annotation of the scholiast: ὦ (ὡς M) γῆ, νοεῖς [O earth, you understand].
κοννεῖν: to understand. κοννοῦσι: they know
you understand well the barbarian speech, O earth
I understand the heaven-conquering ruin of your wife
beating of the breast; toil, distress

Thus Pauw from the scholiast, who correctly explains σὺν κοπετῷ [with beating of the breast], which is said especially of women lamenting and beating their breasts or striking them with their hands: see Thes. vol. 4 p. 1810. In M συγκύπωι, changed by a second hand to σὺν κύπτωι: whence Arnaldus σὺν κτύπῳ [with a crash].

i.e. O Zeus, do not pity us only when we have been utterly overwhelmed by toils and distresses. Thus rightly Schuetz, following the scholiast, μὴ μετὰ τὸ ἀπολέσαι οἰκτειρήσης (οἰκτείρήσεις M, οἰκτειρήσης apogr. Guelf.) ἡμᾶς [do not pity us after destroying us].
escort of libations with sharp hand and beating
O Zeus, pity our toils, and not those who have perished
why, hearing the man-slaying toil, alas, do you not come to our aid?
to strike, smite; to hurt; to beat the breast
